2&#47;3&#47;2026</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 14 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">EXHIBIT 10.11</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:24pt;padding-left:126pt;padding-right:126pt;text-align:center;text-indent:-252pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%;text-decoration:underline">ATTACHMENT 2</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Equalization </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Introduction</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">This Attachment regarding tax reimbursement for business travel relating to Restaurant Brands International US Services LLC (the &#8220;Company&#8221;) or any of its affiliates in more than one (1) tax jurisdiction is called &#8220;tax equalization&#8221;.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Objective</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The objective of tax equalization is to ensure that business travel required to perform the executive&#8217;s roles and responsibilities in more than one (1) tax jurisdiction neither adds significantly to the executive&#8217;s tax liability nor results in significant tax savings due to differences in income and social tax costs between the State of Florida, USA, and the other jurisdiction(s) where the executive may incur individual income taxes due to his or her multi-jurisdictional business travel.  It ensures that the executive&#8217;s out-of-pocket obligations remain approximately the same as they would have been had the executive remained employed only in the State of Florida, USA.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In cases where an executive&#8217;s U.S. tax liabilities are reduced through the use of foreign tax credits or a claim of right under Section 1341 of the United States Internal Revenue Code (as may be amended or superseded), any resulting tax savings of US$100,000 or less that remain after the initial year in which such credits or claims have been utilized will be considered insignificant for purposes of this Attachment 2 and therefore not subject to repayment by the executive.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Reason for Tax Equalization</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The actual tax the executive is expected to incur due to multi-jurisdictional business travel may differ from the amount of tax the executive pays during employment solely in the State of Florida, USA.  The change results from three independent factors&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The amount of tax on employment income, in some cases, significantly increases due to increased tax rates in other jurisdictions&#59;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The executive is usually subject to taxation and the tax regulations (types of income taxed, tax rates, etc.) of international jurisdictions, which differ, often significantly, from those in the State of Florida, USA&#59; and</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The executive is expected to travel between the offices of the Company and its affiliates, and a portion of the costs associated with such travel may be considered taxable income, resulting in significant increases in the executive&#8217;s taxable income over that which would apply if the executive were to have one (1) regular place of employment in the State of Florida, USA.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The result is often that the executive&#8217;s worldwide tax liability may increase significantly.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Scope</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">This tax equalization is limited to income and social taxes on employment income from the Company.  The policy specifically excludes all other taxes such as inheritance&#47;estate tax, gift tax, sales tax or VAT, and property tax. </font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 15 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">EXHIBIT 10.11</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:-27pt"><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Equalization Methodology</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company-designated tax consultant will determine the appropriate method to ensure the executive and the Company pay their fair share of the taxes incurred during the executive&#8217;s multi-jurisdictional business travel.  The executive&#8217;s share of the tax burden is called &#8220;hypothetical tax&#8221; (see below).</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The appropriate approach will depend on whether there are multi-jurisdictional tax liabilities as a result of the multi-jurisdictional business travel.  Whether or not there will be tax liabilities in more than one (1) jurisdiction will depend on the locations and circumstances involved, such as whether there is a tax treaty between the two countries. </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The methodology chosen will involve one or more of the following&#58;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:6pt;margin-top:6pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The executive continues to have actual home-country taxes deducted from their pay&#59;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:6pt;margin-top:6pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">&#8220;Hypothetical tax&#8221; (see below) is deducted from the executive&#8217;s pay&#59; or</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:6pt;margin-top:6pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The Company pays the U.S. tax liability and&#47;or Canadian or other jurisdictional tax liability on &#8220;tax-equalized income&#8221; (see below).</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Overview of the Tax Equalization Process</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company&#8217;s designated tax assistance provider will determine an estimate of the executive&#8217;s hypothetical tax.  Preliminary hypothetical taxes are projected for the year based on hypothetical U.S. income and applicable deductions.  Hypothetical tax is retained from each paycheck throughout the year.  In exchange, the Company pays the executive&#8217;s actual Canadian (or other jurisdictional) and U.S. taxes, if applicable, during the applicable employment period.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Once the Company&#8217;s designated tax assistance provider completes the tax returns for the year, a tax equalization calculation is computed.  This ensures that the executive&#8217;s obligation regarding tax has been met.  This calculation results in a balance due to or from the Company.  The settlement of this balance represents the completion of the year&#8217;s tax equalization process.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Hypothetical Tax&#58; Calculation and Process</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Hypothetical tax is, as stated earlier, the portion of the overall tax liability for which the executive is responsible.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Calculation</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The executive will have their hypothetical tax calculated based on the executive&#8217;s &#8220;normal&#8221; residency within the State of Florida, USA for both income and social taxes considering the relevant filing status and position (for example, marital status and number of dependents, etc.).  This includes any applicable local government jurisdictions (such as state, province, canton, city, municipality, etc.).  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The deductions and credits used to calculate hypothetical tax may vary depending on whether or not the executive continues to have an ongoing tax filing obligation in the United States (e.g., U.S. citizens or permanent residents).</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 16 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr hypothetical itemized deduction.</font></div><div style="padding-left:18pt;padding-right:18pt"><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Withholding</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">If it is determined that the executive should have hypothetical tax withheld, it is calculated by the Company-designated tax consultant upon receipt of instructions from the Company.  This estimated hypothetical tax is pro-rated based on the number of pay periods in the year and is retained from each paycheck throughout the year. In exchange, the Company pays the actual U.S. and Canadian (or other jurisdictional) taxes during (and relating to) the employment period. </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Estimated hypothetical taxes are calculated at the beginning of the employment period and are usually revised once a year after pay increases have been implemented, or upon other salary adjustments.  Additional revisions will be necessary for any executive that experiences a relevant change in his or her situation (e.g. change in marital status, birth of a child, etc.).  The executive should advise the designated tax consultant promptly of any significant change in the executive&#8217;s circumstances in order to calculate the necessary change in estimated hypothetical tax withholding.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The executive will be responsible for hypothetical U.S. tax on special compensation items, in addition to base salary, which would have been paid if the executive had remained in State of Florida, USA, such as incentive compensation (e.g., bonuses).  Accordingly, hypothetical tax will be retained from such compensation when paid.  The Company and the designated tax consultant will determine the appropriate withholding rate on such items.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Types of Income Included in Tax Equalization</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Company Income</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The executive is responsible for hypothetical tax on Company income that the executive would have received had they worked only in State of Florida, USA (&#8220;stay-at-home&#8221; income).  Additionally, the executive is responsible for the U.S. taxes on any shared savings payments and hardship allowances.  The &#8220;stay-at-home&#8221; Company income includes the following&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Salary (less pretax deductions)</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Incentive compensation&#59; and</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Income from exercises or settlements of Company-awarded equity compensation realized during the employment period.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company is responsible for all actual U.S. and Canadian income taxes and social taxes assessed on income associated with the executive&#8217;s business travel (with the exception of shared savings payments and hardship </font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 17 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">EXHIBIT 10.11</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">allowances).  The Company is also responsible for actual Canadian tax which may be payable on the &#8220;stay-at-home&#8221; Company income as outlined above, and on shared savings payments and hardship allowances.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Non-Company Income</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Generally, the executive is responsible for all taxes (U.S. and Canadian (and other jurisdictional)) on all non-Company and non-Affiliate income.  This includes, but is not limited to&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Investment income (such as interest, dividends, and income from rental properties, partnerships, etc.)&#59;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Non-Company and non-Affiliate employment income (including employment or self-employment earnings from a working spouse)&#59;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Income derived from the sale of real property (e.g., capital gains)&#59; and</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Income relating to currency gains related to mortgage transactions.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">However, where the executive is taxed on investment income in Canada or another jurisdiction due to no action taken by the executive, the Company will tax equalize up to $50,000 of this income.  This excludes income from exercises or settlements of Company-awarded equity compensation realized during the employment period, which is equalized as provided above.  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Action taken by the executive that could result in Canada (or another jurisdiction) taxing the income includes remitting such income into Canada (or such other jurisdiction), or realizing a capital gain. The executive should contact the Company-designated tax consultant before taking any action that may result in the generation of tax in Canada (or such other jurisdiction).  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Retirement Plans</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In some instances, Canada may assess an income tax on the earnings in retirement-related accounts, such as pension plans.  As the Company recognizes that executives need to protect such income from inadvertent taxation until retirement, the Company will pay any Canada tax levied in this regard. </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Spousal Income</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">If the executive's spouse decides to work in Canada or any other jurisdiction where the executive&#8217;s compensation is being equalized, the spouse will bear Canadian (or such other jurisdiction&#8217;s) tax costs (and any U.S. taxes, if applicable) associated with such income.  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In the event that the executive and spouse file a joint Canada tax return (or a joint tax return in any jurisdiction other than the U.S., for U.S. taxes) a determination will be made as to whether the Company has funded through estimated tax payments or balance due payment any of the spouse&#8217;s share of Canadian or such other tax.  If the Company has funded any of the spouse&#8217;s liability, the executive will be required to reimburse the Company.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">If the executive&#8217;s spouse is employed outside the United States by an entity other than the Company or one of its affiliates and the spouse is covered by the other entity&#8217;s tax equalization policy, the manner in which the tax equalization calculation and reimbursable taxes are calculated will be determined on a case-by-case basis.  This approach will ensure that the executive receives the tax equalization benefit to which he or she is entitled by eliminating any distorted results that could occur if the standard calculations were performed. </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 18 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">EXHIBIT 10.11</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Estimated Tax Payments, Interest, and Penalties</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company is only responsible for any interest or penalties associated with Company income (and that of its affiliates), assuming the executive has adhered to their responsibilities.  The executive is responsible for all other interest and penalties (e.g. those that accrue due to the executive missing a filing deadline).</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Social Taxes</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Social taxes may exist in Canada as well as the United States.  In order to avoid double taxation, many countries have signed &#8220;totalization agreements&#8221; (social security treaties).  If the United States and Canada have entered into a totalization agreement, then the executive will not be subject to social taxes in both countries but will pay into one only, usually the United States.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">However, no matter what the actual social security liabilities are, the executive will only be responsible for hypothetical U.S. social taxes on &#8220;stay-at-home&#8221; Company income (and that of its affiliates), and the Company will pay all actual social taxes on such income.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Final Settlement</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Equalization Calculation</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">As previously stated, the tax equalization settlements are prepared annually after the preparation of the executive&#8217;s tax returns, using final income and other relevant data, in order to&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Calculate and reconcile the executive&#8217;s final hypothetical tax responsibility&#59; and</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Allocate all actual Canadian taxes and the taxes of other jurisdictions to the extent subject to equalization pursuant to the Agreement and this Attachment 2 (and any U.S. taxes, if applicable) between the executive and the Company.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Tax equalization calculations are prepared by the Company-designated tax consultant to ensure consistency and proper application of Company policy.  The Company-designated tax consultant will send the Company a copy of the summary tax data from the equalization for processing at the time the equalization is mailed or delivered to the executive. The tax equalization settlement usually results in an amount due to&#47;from the executive.  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Any payments due to the Company from the executive must be settled within 30 days of the later of&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Receipt of the tax equalization calculation&#59; or</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Receipt of any refund due to the executive by the U.S. and&#47;or Canadian or other applicable taxing authorities.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company also reserves the right to stop the payment of assignment allowances or deduct outstanding balances from bonus or termination payments in order to collect unpaid equalization balances.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Actual Tax Return Balances</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Upon receipt of the completed tax returns, the executive is expected to pay any balance due.  Conversely, if the actual returns generate a refund, the executive will collect the refund.  Both balances due and refunds owed will be included as part of the tax equalization settlement (see above).</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company may, at its discretion, make direct payments to the taxing authorities on behalf of the executive for taxes owed when the tax is the Company&#8217;s responsibility, as determined by the tax equalization settlement.  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 19 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">EXHIBIT 10.11</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Credits</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Any tax credits for taxes paid by the Company, which reduced the executive&#8217;s income tax liability before, during, or subsequent to his or her employment are owned&#47;utilized by the Company.  After multi-jurisdictional business travel on behalf of the Company or its affiliates terminates (including by reason of termination of executive&#8217;s employment with the Company), the Company determines whether to keep the executive in the tax equalization program if the executive has carryover tax credits that may be used in the future.  The Company retains the tax benefit for utilization of the tax credit.  The Company continues to pay for the preparation of the executive&#8217;s home-country income tax return during these years.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> </font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Preparation Assistance</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">It is the Company&#8217;s policy that all executives who have multi-jurisdictional business travel comply fully with all applicable laws and regulations relating to filing procedures and payment of taxes.  Therefore, the Company provides executives who have multi-jurisdictional business travel with the services of a Company-designated tax consultant to assist in preparing U.S. and Canadian tax returns for the duration of the employment period and, if necessary, the year after termination.  Tax returns will also be prepared on behalf of the accompanying spouse&#47;partner if separate returns are legally required.  The executive is responsible for complying with all requirements regarding personal tax filings and payments to each taxing authority to which any such requirement exists.  If an executive fails to provide required tax information, any resulting penalties or interest will be borne by the executive.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 20 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div></body></html>

(i) if the Achievement Price equals or exceeds the Target Amount during the Initial Measurement Period, the number of Earned Performance Units will not be less than Target Amount, subject to the style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%;text-decoration:underline">ATTACHMENT 2</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:center"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Equalization </font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Introduction</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">This Attachment regarding tax reimbursement for business travel relating to Restaurant Brands International US Services LLC (the &#8220;Company&#8221;) or any of its affiliates in more than one (1) tax jurisdiction is called &#8220;tax equalization&#8221;.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Objective</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The objective of tax equalization is to ensure that business travel required to perform the executive&#8217;s roles and responsibilities in more than one (1) tax jurisdiction neither adds significantly to the executive&#8217;s tax liability nor results in significant tax savings due to differences in income and social tax costs between the State of Florida, USA, and the other jurisdiction(s) where the executive may incur individual income taxes due to his or her multi-jurisdictional business travel.  It ensures that the executive&#8217;s out-of-pocket obligations remain approximately the same as they would have been had the executive remained employed only in the State of Florida, USA.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In cases where an executive&#8217;s U.S. tax liabilities are reduced through the use of foreign tax credits or a claim of right under Section 1341 of the United States Internal Revenue Code (as may be amended or superseded), any resulting tax savings of US$100,000 or less that remain after the initial year in which such credits or claims have been utilized will be considered insignificant for purposes of this Attachment 2 and therefore not subject to repayment by the executive.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Reason for Tax Equalization</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The actual tax the executive is expected to incur due to multi-jurisdictional business travel may differ from the amount of tax the executive pays during employment solely in the State of Florida, USA.  The change results from three independent factors&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The amount of tax on employment income, in some cases, significantly increases due to increased tax rates in other jurisdictions&#59;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The executive is usually subject to taxation and the tax regulations (types of income taxed, tax rates, etc.) of international jurisdictions, which differ, often significantly, from those in the State of Florida, USA&#59; and</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The executive is expected to travel between the offices of the Company and its affiliates, and a portion of the costs associated with such travel may be considered taxable income, resulting in significant increases in the executive&#8217;s taxable income over that which would apply if the executive were to have one (1) regular place of employment in the State of Florida, USA.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The result is often that the executive&#8217;s worldwide tax liability may increase significantly.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Scope</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">This tax equalization is limited to income and social taxes on employment income from the Company.  The policy specifically excludes all other taxes such as inheritance&#47;estate tax, gift tax, sales tax or VAT, and property tax. </font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 15 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">EXHIBIT 10.18</font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify;text-indent:-27pt"><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Equalization Methodology</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company-designated tax consultant will determine the appropriate method to ensure the executive and the Company pay their fair share of the taxes incurred during the executive&#8217;s multi-jurisdictional business travel.  The executive&#8217;s share of the tax burden is called &#8220;hypothetical tax&#8221; (see below).</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The appropriate approach will depend on whether there are multi-jurisdictional tax liabilities as a result of the multi-jurisdictional business travel.  Whether or not there will be tax liabilities in more than one (1) jurisdiction will depend on the locations and circumstances involved, such as whether there is a tax treaty between the two countries. </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The methodology chosen will involve one or more of the following&#58;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:6pt;margin-top:6pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The executive continues to have actual home-country taxes deducted from their pay&#59;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:6pt;margin-top:6pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">&#8220;Hypothetical tax&#8221; (see below) is deducted from the executive&#8217;s pay&#59; or</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:6pt;margin-top:6pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">The Company pays the U.S. tax liability and&#47;or Canadian or other jurisdictional tax liability on &#8220;tax-equalized income&#8221; (see below).</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Overview of the Tax Equalization Process</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company&#8217;s designated tax assistance provider will determine an estimate of the executive&#8217;s hypothetical tax.  Preliminary hypothetical taxes are projected for the year based on hypothetical U.S. income and applicable deductions.  Hypothetical tax is retained from each paycheck throughout the year.  In exchange, the Company pays the executive&#8217;s actual Canadian (or other jurisdictional) and U.S. taxes, if applicable, during the applicable employment period.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Once the Company&#8217;s designated tax assistance provider completes the tax returns for the year, a tax equalization calculation is computed.  This ensures that the executive&#8217;s obligation regarding tax has been met.  This calculation results in a balance due to or from the Company.  The settlement of this balance represents the completion of the year&#8217;s tax equalization process.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Hypothetical Tax&#58; Calculation and Process</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Hypothetical tax is, as stated earlier, the portion of the overall tax liability for which the executive is responsible.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Calculation</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The executive will have their hypothetical tax calculated based on the executive&#8217;s &#8220;normal&#8221; residency within the State of Florida, USA for both income and social taxes considering the relevant filing status and position (for example, marital status and number of dependents, etc.).  This includes any applicable local government jurisdictions (such as state, province, canton, city, municipality, etc.).  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The deductions and credits used to calculate hypothetical tax may vary depending on whether or not the executive continues to have an ongoing tax filing obligation in the United States (e.g., U.S. citizens or permanent residents).</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 16 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="text-align:right"><font (marital, family, filing, etc.).</font></td></tr></table></div><div style="padding-left:18pt;padding-right:18pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">*For U.S. executives, hypothetical state and city tax replaces actual state and city taxes as a hypothetical itemized deduction.</font></div><div style="padding-left:18pt;padding-right:18pt"><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Withholding</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">If it is determined that the executive should have hypothetical tax withheld, it is calculated by the Company-designated tax consultant upon receipt of instructions from the Company.  This estimated hypothetical tax is pro-rated based on the number of pay periods in the year and is retained from each paycheck throughout the year. In exchange, the Company pays the actual U.S. and Canadian (or other jurisdictional) taxes during (and relating to) the employment period. </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Estimated hypothetical taxes are calculated at the beginning of the employment period and are usually revised once a year after pay increases have been implemented, or upon other salary adjustments.  Additional revisions will be necessary for any executive that experiences a relevant change in his or her situation (e.g. change in marital status, birth of a child, etc.).  The executive should advise the designated tax consultant promptly of any significant change in the executive&#8217;s circumstances in order to calculate the necessary change in estimated hypothetical tax withholding.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The executive will be responsible for hypothetical U.S. tax on special compensation items, in addition to base salary, which would have been paid if the executive had remained in State of Florida, USA, such as incentive compensation (e.g., bonuses).  Accordingly, hypothetical tax will be retained from such compensation when paid.  The Company and the designated tax consultant will determine the appropriate withholding rate on such items.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Types of Income Included in Tax Equalization</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Company Income</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The executive is responsible for hypothetical tax on Company income that the executive would have received had they worked only in State of Florida, USA (&#8220;stay-at-home&#8221; income).  Additionally, the executive is responsible for the U.S. taxes on any shared savings payments and hardship allowances.  The &#8220;stay-at-home&#8221; Company income includes the following&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Salary (less pretax deductions)</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Incentive compensation&#59; and</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Income from exercises or settlements of Company-awarded equity compensation realized during the employment period.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company is responsible for all actual U.S. and Canadian income taxes and social taxes assessed on income associated with the executive&#8217;s business travel (with the exception of shared savings payments and hardship </font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 17 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">EXHIBIT 10.18</font></div></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">allowances).  The Company is also responsible for actual Canadian tax which may be payable on the &#8220;stay-at-home&#8221; Company income as outlined above, and on shared savings payments and hardship allowances.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Non-Company Income</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Generally, the executive is responsible for all taxes (U.S. and Canadian (and other jurisdictional)) on all non-Company and non-Affiliate income.  This includes, but is not limited to&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Investment income (such as interest, dividends, and income from rental properties, partnerships, etc.)&#59;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Non-Company and non-Affiliate employment income (including employment or self-employment earnings from a working spouse)&#59;</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Income derived from the sale of real property (e.g., capital gains)&#59; and</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Income relating to currency gains related to mortgage transactions.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">However, where the executive is taxed on investment income in Canada or another jurisdiction due to no action taken by the executive, the Company will tax equalize up to $50,000 of this income.  This excludes income from exercises or settlements of Company-awarded equity compensation realized during the employment period, which is equalized as provided above.  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Action taken by the executive that could result in Canada (or another jurisdiction) taxing the income includes remitting such income into Canada (or such other jurisdiction), or realizing a capital gain. The executive should contact the Company-designated tax consultant before taking any action that may result in the generation of tax in Canada (or such other jurisdiction).  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Retirement Plans</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In some instances, Canada may assess an income tax on the earnings in retirement-related accounts, such as pension plans.  As the Company recognizes that executives need to protect such income from inadvertent taxation until retirement, the Company will pay any Canada tax levied in this regard. </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Spousal Income</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">If the executive's spouse decides to work in Canada or any other jurisdiction where the executive&#8217;s compensation is being equalized, the spouse will bear Canadian (or such other jurisdiction&#8217;s) tax costs (and any U.S. taxes, if applicable) associated with such income.  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">In the event that the executive and spouse file a joint Canada tax return (or a joint tax return in any jurisdiction other than the U.S., for U.S. taxes) a determination will be made as to whether the Company has funded through estimated tax payments or balance due payment any of the spouse&#8217;s share of Canadian or such other tax.  If the Company has funded any of the spouse&#8217;s liability, the executive will be required to reimburse the Company.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">If the executive&#8217;s spouse is employed outside the United States by an entity other than the Company or one of its affiliates and the spouse is covered by the other entity&#8217;s tax equalization policy, the manner in which the tax equalization calculation and reimbursable taxes are calculated will be determined on a case-by-case basis.  This approach will ensure that the executive receives the tax equalization benefit to which he or she is entitled by eliminating any distorted results that could occur if the standard calculations were performed. </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 18 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">EXHIBIT 10.18</font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Estimated Tax Payments, Interest, and Penalties</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company is only responsible for any interest or penalties associated with Company income (and that of its affiliates), assuming the executive has adhered to their responsibilities.  The executive is responsible for all other interest and penalties (e.g. those that accrue due to the executive missing a filing deadline).</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Social Taxes</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Social taxes may exist in Canada as well as the United States.  In order to avoid double taxation, many countries have signed &#8220;totalization agreements&#8221; (social security treaties).  If the United States and Canada have entered into a totalization agreement, then the executive will not be subject to social taxes in both countries but will pay into one only, usually the United States.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">However, no matter what the actual social security liabilities are, the executive will only be responsible for hypothetical U.S. social taxes on &#8220;stay-at-home&#8221; Company income (and that of its affiliates), and the Company will pay all actual social taxes on such income.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Final Settlement</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Equalization Calculation</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">As previously stated, the tax equalization settlements are prepared annually after the preparation of the executive&#8217;s tax returns, using final income and other relevant data, in order to&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Calculate and reconcile the executive&#8217;s final hypothetical tax responsibility&#59; and</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Allocate all actual Canadian taxes and the taxes of other jurisdictions to the extent subject to equalization pursuant to the Agreement and this Attachment 2 (and any U.S. taxes, if applicable) between the executive and the Company.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Tax equalization calculations are prepared by the Company-designated tax consultant to ensure consistency and proper application of Company policy.  The Company-designated tax consultant will send the Company a copy of the summary tax data from the equalization for processing at the time the equalization is mailed or delivered to the executive. The tax equalization settlement usually results in an amount due to&#47;from the executive.  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Any payments due to the Company from the executive must be settled within 30 days of the later of&#58;</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Receipt of the tax equalization calculation&#59; or</font></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;padding-left:17pt;text-indent:-17pt"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Wingdings',sans-serif;font-size:9pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">n</font><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%;padding-left:10.29pt">Receipt of any refund due to the executive by the U.S. and&#47;or Canadian or other applicable taxing authorities.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company also reserves the right to stop the payment of assignment allowances or deduct outstanding balances from bonus or termination payments in order to collect unpaid equalization balances.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11.5pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Actual Tax Return Balances</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Upon receipt of the completed tax returns, the executive is expected to pay any balance due.  Conversely, if the actual returns generate a refund, the executive will collect the refund.  Both balances due and refunds owed will be included as part of the tax equalization settlement (see above).</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">The Company may, at its discretion, make direct payments to the taxing authorities on behalf of the executive for taxes owed when the tax is the Company&#8217;s responsibility, as determined by the tax equalization settlement.  </font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 19 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div style="min-height:90pt;width:100%"><div><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">EXHIBIT 10.18</font></div></div><div style="margin-bottom:12pt;text-align:justify"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Credits</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">Any tax credits for taxes paid by the Company, which reduced the executive&#8217;s income tax liability before, during, or subsequent to his or her employment are owned&#47;utilized by the Company.  After multi-jurisdictional business travel on behalf of the Company or its affiliates terminates (including by reason of termination of executive&#8217;s employment with the Company), the Company determines whether to keep the executive in the tax equalization program if the executive has carryover tax credits that may be used in the future.  The Company retains the tax benefit for utilization of the tax credit.  The Company continues to pay for the preparation of the executive&#8217;s home-country income tax return during these years.</font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Arial',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%"> </font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-style:italic;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Tax Preparation Assistance</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:10pt;font-weight:400;line-height:120%">It is the Company&#8217;s policy that all executives who have multi-jurisdictional business travel comply fully with all applicable laws and regulations relating to filing procedures and payment of taxes.  Therefore, the Company provides executives who have multi-jurisdictional business travel with the services of a Company-designated tax consultant to assist in preparing U.S. and Canadian tax returns for the duration of the employment period and, if necessary, the year after termination.  Tax returns will also be prepared on behalf of the accompanying spouse&#47;partner if separate returns are legally required.  The executive is responsible for complying with all requirements regarding personal tax filings and payments to each taxing authority to which any such requirement exists.  If an executive fails to provide required tax information, any resulting penalties or interest will be borne by the executive.</font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="text-align:justify"><font><br></font></div><div><font><br></font></div><div style="height:72pt;position:relative;width:100%"><div style="bottom:0;position:absolute;width:100%"><div style="text-align:right"><font style="color:#000000;font-family:'Calibri',sans-serif;font-size:11pt;font-weight:700;line-height:120%">Page 20 of 20</font></div><div style="text-align:center"><font><br></font></div></div></div></body></html>
